title: Detect drift
description: Change the database behind the schema file's back, then ask Ptah what differs and read the exit code.

files.schema.sql:
-- The schema you want the database to have.
--
-- Ptah reads this file as the desired state, reads the real catalog out of
-- app.db, and works out the difference. You never write ALTER statements here.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  title   TEXT NOT NULL,
  done    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id)
);
files.README.md:
# Workspace

    schema.sql   the schema you want
    app.db       the SQLite database you have

This time schema.sql stays as it is. The database is what changes.

Run drift first, so you can see it clean:

    ptah schema drift --schema-file schema.sql --db-url sqlite://app.db

Then change the database directly, in the SQL pane:

    ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN nickname TEXT;

Nothing told schema.sql about that. Run drift again and read the exit code.
0 means in sync, 1 means drifted, 2 means Ptah could not decide.

baseline.message: This route expects a users table in app.db and a schema.sql in the workspace. One of them is gone, so the steps below no longer describe what you have. Everything still works; Reset puts the scenario back.

steps.title: Start in sync
steps.caption: Desired = actual
steps.headline: In sync is what a deploy pipeline wants to see.
steps.instruction: Establish the baseline. schema.sql and app.db describe the same tables, so drift has nothing to report.
steps.done: Exit 0. This is the state a deploy pipeline would want to see.

steps.title: Change the DB
steps.caption: DDL in the SQL pane
steps.headline: Change the database directly, the way a hotfix does.
steps.instruction: Add a column straight to the database, the way a hotfix or a hand-run migration would. schema.sql is not touched.

action.sql: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN nickname TEXT;

steps.done: The catalog has users.nickname and schema.sql does not mention it. That gap is drift, and a drift run that exits 1 keeps proving it happened even after the column is put back.

steps.title: Run drift
steps.caption: Real exit code
steps.headline: Ask the same question again and read the number.
steps.instruction: Ask the same question as in step 1. The command is identical; only the database changed.
steps.done: Exit 1 is a negative check result, not a tool failure. The command worked and answered no.

steps.title: Read the report
steps.caption: The findings as data
steps.headline: Read the same report as data, the way a pipeline would.
steps.instruction: Ask again with --format json. The findings are the same, now as data: each with its severity, and the column by name, nickname in users under columns_removed. It counts as removed because making the database match schema.sql would drop it, and that is why it is destructive.
steps.done: Exit 1 again, with the same finding as data: columns_removed, destructive, users.nickname. That JSON is what a CI job reads.

steps.title: Reconcile
steps.caption: Edit schema or revert
steps.headline: Adopt the change or revert it, then check again.
steps.instruction: Two honest ways out: adopt the column by adding nickname to schema.sql, or drop it in the SQL pane. Either way, run drift again to prove it.
steps.done: Reconciled, and checked by a drift run that happened after the reconciliation rather than before it.

finished.headline: Drift is a question with three answers: 0, 1 and 2.
finished.caption: Run this in CI against a real database and you learn about the gap before your users do.
